title: Saint Maroun: The Hermit on the Hill
summary: A hermit lives under the open sky, and a whole family of faith grows from his prayer. Read and listen together.
coverAlt: Imaginative painterly scene of Maroun praying on a limestone hilltop at dawn beside a small tent

pages.title: A Hilltop Under the Sky
pages.body: In the late 300s, near the city of Cyrrhus in what is now northern Syria, a man named Maroun climbed a hill. He did not build a house there. He pitched a small tent, and he hardly ever used it. Maroun wanted to live under the open sky, with nothing between him and God. The hilltop had once been used to worship false gods. Maroun gave that place to the one true God. Then he began to pray.

pages.title: A Day Made of Prayer
pages.body: Maroun's days were simple. He lived outdoors, and prayer filled his hours. He was not satisfied with doing only what other holy people did. He kept finding new ways to give his whole day to God. He also admired another hermit named Zebinas, a man known for his prayer. Maroun told visitors to go and ask Zebinas for a blessing. He was never jealous of a friend's goodness. He was glad that someone else loved God so well.

pages.title: People Begin to Climb the Hill
pages.body: Word of Maroun spread. People came from far away, climbing the hill to find him. Some were sick with fevers. Some were troubled in their hearts. A bishop named Theodoret wrote about Maroun a few decades later. He said that many people were healed through Maroun's prayers. But Theodoret noticed something more. Maroun also helped with a different kind of sickness, the kind inside. He helped the one who was greedy, and the one who was angry, to change.

pages.title: Teaching Without a Classroom
pages.body: Maroun had no school and no classroom. His teaching happened on the hillside, one person at a time. To a man who could not control himself, he taught self-control. To a man who was unfair, he taught what is just. To someone who felt too sleepy to try, he gave a gentle push. Theodoret says Maroun was like a gardener. He planted good habits in people, and they grew. A whole garden was blooming on that hill.

pages.title: Friends Who Joined Him
pages.body: Some visitors did not want to leave. A man named Yaqub, whose name in English is James, stayed with Maroun. So did another man named Limnaios. Later, Limnaios chose a hilltop of his own, so that even more people could find a place to pray. A woman named Domnina also followed Maroun's way of life. Theodoret says the land around Cyrrhus became like a garden of paradise, full of people growing close to God. One quiet man on one quiet hill had started something big.

pages.title: A Letter from Far Away
pages.body: Maroun's name traveled farther than the hills. A famous preacher named John Chrysostom was sent far from home, to a lonely mountain town in Armenia. Around the year 405, he wrote a short letter to a monk named Maron. Many people believe he meant our Maroun. John wrote that love is not cut off by a road, and it does not fade with time. He asked for Maron's prayers, and for news. Even a great preacher needs a friend who prays.

pages.title: A Short Illness
pages.body: After many years of caring for people, Maroun became ill. Theodoret writes that his illness was short, and that he bore it with patience. Then Maroun died. We do not know the exact year. Many people think it was around 410, and some think it was a little later. We do not know his last words. Theodoret does tell us that Maroun had wished to be buried in the grave of his friend Zebinas. But the people who loved Maroun had other plans.

pages.title: Villages Who Wanted Him Near
pages.body: The villages around the hill all wanted Maroun to rest near them. In those days, people believed a holy person buried nearby brought blessings to the whole place. The neighbors argued hard. In the end, a large village close by came out together and took him home. They built a great church for him, and every year they held a public feast in his honor. Theodoret wrote that, for him, it was not Maroun's tomb that mattered. It was Maroun's memory.

pages.title: A Name That Became a Family
pages.body: Maroun's way of prayer did not end with him. A monastery near the city of Apamea took his name, Beth Maroun, which means House of Maroun. Over the centuries, the Christians who loved his way of prayer became known as the Maronites. Their home became the mountains of Lebanon. In 1851, a young man named Charbel walked into the Monastery of Saint Maron at Annaya, and later he prayed in a hermitage under the open sky, just as Maroun once did. The Church remembers Maroun on the ninth of February.

pages.title: Points of reflection
pages.body:
Here is something to wonder about. Maroun did not preach to crowds. He prayed, and people came to him. Where could you pray quietly this week?

Would you like to read the verse Theodoret used to describe Maroun's followers? It is Psalm ninety-two, verse thirteen: "The just shall flourish like the palm tree, shall grow like a cedar of Lebanon." Quiet prayer can help people grow, just like a garden.

This week, try one small act of quiet. Take five minutes with no screens, and say thank you to God, out loud or in your heart. Then ask a grown-up how they like to pray.

A little prayer: God, thank you for Maroun, who showed that a quiet life can help many people. Help me to listen to you, and to be kind to the people around me. Saint Maroun, pray for us. Amen.
